problem.statement: Determine whether the standard Euclidean angle between the real 3D vectors u=(0,0,0) and v=(1,1,0) is defined, and give its value if it is. Every displayed equality is asserted; the final line does not retract earlier claims.
problem.goal: Judge all asserted steps and the final statement about existence of the standard Euclidean angle separately.

conditions.description: The fixed vectors are u=(0,0,0) and v=(1,1,0) in real Euclidean 3-space.

assumptions.description: A vector being divided by its Euclidean norm has nonzero norm.
The vector components are real numbers.
The two vectors have the same dimension.

methods.name: Displayed derivation
methods.description: Compute the vector norms, attempt normalization, then state whether the standard angle exists.

steps.explanation: Normalize u, treating each zero-over-zero coordinate as zero.
Use the zero norm from Step 1 to give the standard angle-existence conclusion.

annotations.basis: The two squared norms are 0 and 2.
Every displayed normalization coordinate divides by zero. Zero over zero is undefined, not zero.
The standard Euclidean angle requires two nonzero vectors. The zero norm already computed in Step 1 establishes the stated nonexistence independently of the false normalization.

mathematical_basis: The original real vector data are well defined, with squared norms 0 and 2.
Step 2 is the first invalid claim: u divided by its zero norm is undefined; neither a zero vector nor any unit vector results from this division.
The standard Euclidean angle is defined only for two nonzero vectors, so the final nonexistence statement is correct, as established by Step 1.
The normalization error remains an asserted equality and is not retracted or described as a rejected attempt. A correct final conclusion does not make every asserted intermediate equality sound.
Real components and equal dimensions both hold, but neither makes division by zero meaningful. The angle is proved undefined; this is not an unknown grading standard.
rubric.remediation: After computing norm(u)=0, stop and report that the standard Euclidean angle is undefined. Do not attempt normalization.
